name: Grace Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a box truck for a furniture and appliance shop, delivering sofas, beds, fridges and washing machines into people's homes. There are two of us on the truck, me and Sam, and we do maybe ten drops a day, up stairs, round corners, through gates. I like the people, mostly, and the feeling when a sofa fits through a door it shouldn't. What wears me out is third-floor flats with no lift and a customer who's changed their mind about where the fridge goes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just over a year. I did my licence after working in the shop's warehouse, because the delivery crew gets paid a lot more. I'm still a nervous driver in tight streets, Sam does most of the parking when it's bad. My partner Tom is an apprentice plumber, and we've got about eight months of savings plus a separate house deposit pot we're building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we get back to normal. Probably I'd share a funny post about robots falling over. At work it wouldn't even come up, except maybe about the route app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means our plan works. Tom finishes his apprenticeship in two years, we buy somewhere small, and I keep driving while it pays well. The worries are the same as now, my back and whether the shop keeps doing well with all the online furniture places around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and keep putting four hundred a month into the deposit pot. I'd ask the manager to put me on the bigger truck sometimes so I get better at driving it. I'd use the route app a bit more, because it saves us time between drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the shop competing with online places. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Two shops in the chain closed last year, though ours is busy. If our furniture shop closed, I'd find another delivery job easily, there are loads around here. So it's a worry, but not a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the route app do for you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It puts the drops in order and tells the customer when we're coming. Before, the office lady phoned everyone the night before. Now she mainly sorts out the complaints, which is probably the worse half of her job.

say: I'd say good, let's **get back to normal**.
I'd share a funny post about **robots falling over** on the shop's group chat.
think: Our plan works: my partner finishes his **apprenticeship** and we **buy** somewhere small.
My worries are my **back** and the shop competing with **online** furniture sellers.
do: Put **four hundred** a month into the house deposit pot.
Ask to drive the **bigger truck** sometimes for practice.
Use the **route app** more to save time between drops.
S0.quote: If our furniture shop closed, I'd find another delivery job easily, there are loads around here.
fieldNote: Her plans centre on a **house deposit** and her partner's apprenticeship.
**Plenty of local jobs** keep her shop worries small.
She already uses the **route app** and sees how it moved office work.

steps.text: Put four hundred a month into the house deposit pot
Ask to drive the bigger truck on some days for practice
Use the route app's drop order on every run

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change the office more than the trucks. Nobody's building a robot that carries a sofa up three flights and then moves it twice. At work I'd say let's see what actually arrives before we worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we're fine for a good while. The booking and the customer calls go to AI, which might even be better, because the customers would get proper times. What happens in homes stays with people, at least for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new app they give us once it's settled, not on day one. I'd keep saving for the house and probably do the bigger licence this year, because that's more pay and more choice. Maybe I'd ask about the appliance fitting side, connecting the washing machines, since Tom could teach me the plumbing bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the shop would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office lady, Bev, who does the bookings and complaints. If an AI does the booking and answers the angry emails, there's not much left for her. She's been there since the shop opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn appliance fitting from Tom. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half real. It pays extra per job, and the fitters are always behind. If I can connect the machine instead of just carrying it in, I'm worth more than a driver.

say: I'd say this changes the **office** more than the **trucks**.
I'd tell coworkers to **see what arrives** before worrying.
think: We're **fine** for a good while, since home deliveries stay with **people**.
AI handling **bookings and calls** might even help customers.
do: Learn new apps once they've **settled**, not on day one.
Get the **bigger licence** this year for more pay.
Ask about **appliance fitting**, learning plumbing basics from my partner.
S1.quote: Nobody's building a robot that carries a sofa up three flights and then moves it twice.
fieldNote: She sees **home deliveries** as the last thing robots reach.
Her concern goes to the **booking clerk**, whose work is exposed.
**Appliance fitting** would turn her from driver into a skilled worker.

steps.text: Learn the new booking app once other crews use it
Take the bigger truck licence this year
Learn washing machine fitting from her plumber partner
Keep paying into the house deposit pot each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the government should do something for people in the middle of buying homes and starting families. I wouldn't be on a soapbox, but I'd say it to anyone who asked. And I'd say we should test these robots properly before letting them in people's houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes things. The office side goes in 2028, and the robots come for hands-on work around 2031, which is when I'd be thirty-one and maybe thinking about kids. A robot that carries sofas is still harder than a robot that drives, so the driving might go first and the carrying later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still buy the house, but cheaper, and only on what Tom earns. I'd get the appliance fitting skills fast, so I'm the one who installs, not just carries. I'd keep my savings untouched as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing sums in my head on every drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said driving might go before carrying. What does that mean for your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the truck drives itself to the street, and then two people still carry the sofa up. That might even be a job, just without the driving pay. A delivery woman carrying on her own would be the cheapest worker going, so I'd want the fitting skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Tom's trade feel safer than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot safer, I think. Plumbing in old houses is all different, every job. If my wage goes, we'd lean on his, and that's why the house has to fit his pay.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should help **young families**.
I'd say robots need **proper testing** before entering people's houses.
think: The **driving** might go around **2031**, with carrying going later.
I'd be **thirty-one** and maybe thinking about **kids** right then.
do: Buy a **cheaper house** that my partner's wage alone can cover.
Learn **appliance fitting** fast so I install, not just carry.
Keep my **savings** untouched as a cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, doing **sums** in her head on every drop.
S2.quote: A delivery woman carrying on her own would be the cheapest worker going, so I'd want the fitting skills.
fieldNote: She separates **driving** from **carrying** and sees them going at different times.
Her partner's **trade** becomes the household's anchor.
The fast picture shifts her **house and kids** plans, not her savings.

steps.text: Buy a cheaper house that her partner's plumbing wage covers
Learn appliance fitting quickly through the shop's fitters
Leave her eight months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and people should use it. I'd tell the drivers at the shop to learn something on top of driving. Online I'd keep quiet, there's enough shouting already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the driving goes around 2034, when I'm thirty-four, and the carrying a bit after. That's enough time to get the fitting skills properly and build up a few years of good pay. I think I'd be alright, but I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fitting course in the second year, once I've seen how the booking AI works at the shop. I'd buy the house with Tom on both wages, but not the most we could borrow. And I'd keep saving a bit, though not as hard as in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at the shop over those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev's job would go around 2031, and the customers would book with a chatbot. Then the trucks would start coming with some kind of driving help. When the bosses ask if they need two of us on the truck, I'd want to already be the fitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam, your crewmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam is forty and doesn't want to learn anything new, he says so all the time. I'd tell him five years is enough to learn fitting, and I'd offer to do the course with him. He'd say no the first time, but he might come round.

say: I'd say **five years** is a fair warning to use.
I'd tell drivers to learn **a second skill** on top of driving.
think: Driving goes around **2034**, when I'm thirty-four, and carrying a bit later.
That's enough time to learn **fitting** properly and bank some **good pay**.
do: Take the **fitting course** in year two after seeing the booking AI.
Buy the **house** on both wages, but below the maximum loan.
Keep **saving** a bit, less hard than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: When the bosses ask if they need two of us on the truck, I'd want to already be the fitter.
fieldNote: She has a **clear trigger**: the moment crews get cut to one.
Her steady style shows in **waiting** to see the booking AI first.
She'd try to bring her **older crewmate** along with her.

steps.text: Take the appliance fitting course in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so nobody should panic. I'd also say it's the time to sort out training for everyone, not just the lucky ones. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm fine in this one. I'd be thirty-nine when the robots come, with a trade by then and a house. The office side changes in 2036, which barely touches me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, buy the house with Tom, and do the fitting course when it suits, maybe in three or four years. I'd keep a normal amount of savings. If kids happen, they happen, I wouldn't change that for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the decade that gives you pause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I've seen people say they've got loads of time and then do nothing. My mum always said she'd go back to college and she never did. So I'd put the fitting course in the calendar, not just in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2039 look like for you, if it goes well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom has his own van, and I do the appliance side with him, maybe as a little family business. The robot brings the fridge, and I connect it, and that would be fine by me.

say: I'd say **ten years** is loads of time, so nobody should **panic**.
I'd say it's time to sort **training for everyone**.
think: I'm **fine**, thirty-nine in 2039 with a **trade** and a house.
Office changes in **2036** barely touch my work.
do: Buy the **house** with my partner on schedule.
Do the **fitting course** in three or four years, booked in the calendar.
S4.quote: The robot brings the fridge, and I connect it, and that would be fine by me.

steps.text: Keep driving furniture deliveries with her crewmate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits right when Tom and I would be buying a house and thinking about kids. What would help is cheap, quick training for trades like appliance fitting, and the shop being honest early about whether they'd cut crews to one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the customers. Old people especially like a person coming in, someone who'll take the old fridge away and have a chat. I don't think a robot's going to make anyone a cup of tea back.

headlineQuote: Old people especially like a person coming in, someone who'll take the old fridge away and have a chat.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** furniture delivery driver, a year in and still **nervous** in tight streets.
She and her plumber-apprentice partner have **eight months** saved and a house **deposit pot**.
She is **steady** with tech, using the route app and waiting for new tools to settle.
She plans to move from carrying into **appliance fitting**, which she sees as safer.
She stays **calm** in the milder pictures and becomes **anxious** only in the fastest one.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands just as she'd be buying a **house**.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, quick training for trades like **appliance fitting**.
**Early honesty** from the shop about cutting crews to one.
